tldr: This study reproduces and scientifically explains counterintuitive mysteries frequently observed in real-world robot behavioral cloning—such as 'overfitting helps performance' and 'open-loop control beats closed-loop'—using 'OCBench', a GPU-accelerated simulator environment that faithfully mimics the properties of human demonstrations.
hero_caption: An overview of the 5 environment suites (block, chamber, switch, hanoi, bowling) and all 28 tasks provided by OCBench. It features diverse manipulation challenges ranging from simple block manipulation and precision Towers of Hanoi to puzzles requiring combinatorial search.
overview:
Behavioral cloning (BC) has become a standard approach in robot learning. However, when trained on large-scale real-world data, several strange, counterintuitive phenomena have been known to occur. For example, task success rates often keep rising as the model overfits, open-loop control using action chunking (predicting and executing actions in blocks) works far better than closed-loop control that responds immediately to current observations, and feeding observation history often degrades performance.

Yet, scientifically investigating these phenomena on real robots was difficult. Human demonstration data collected on real hardware is expensive, making controlled comparisons under identical conditions challenging. Meanwhile, conventional simulator-generated synthetic data somehow failed to clearly exhibit these phenomena. This was because traditional scripted policies (rule-based trajectory generation programs) relied too heavily on Gaussian noise, failing to capture the temporal correlations, narrow distributions, and diverse approaches characteristic of human trajectories.

To address this, the authors built 'OCBench', a new benchmark featuring scripted policies that faithfully reproduce the geometric and temporal structure of human demonstrations. Based on an NVIDIA Warp-accelerated GPU-parallel simulator (MJWarp), it achieves ultra-fast data generation of up to 200,000 steps per second. Using this environment, the authors reproduced four BC mysteries reported in the real world and tested and refuted existing hypotheses, uncovering the underlying mechanisms behind these phenomena.
contributions: Designed scripted policies that reproduce the trajectory smoothness, temporal correlations, and semantic diversity of human demonstrations, building 'OCBench' to reproduce real-world BC behaviors in simulation.
Adopted MJWarp (GPU-parallel MuJoCo) to enable ultra-fast trajectory generation and streaming training at up to 200,000 environment steps per second on a single H100 GPU.

Reproduced four mysteries—the benefits of overfitting, the superiority of open-loop control, the need for huge models, and hypersensitivity to feature scaling—under fully controlled conditions, testing and refuting various hypotheses.

Provided 28 diverse robotic manipulation tasks spanning different difficulty levels and characteristics, including single- and multi-object manipulation, opening drawers and windows, Towers of Hanoi, and bowling.

sections.heading: Can we unravel BC's counterintuitive mysteries in simulation?
sections.summary: While simple, behavioral cloning (BC) exhibits many counterintuitive phenomena on real hardware. Overcoming the limits of costly real-world experiments and uncooperative conventional simulators, the authors propose 'OCBench', a GPU-accelerated benchmark mimicking key properties of human demonstrations.
sections.details:
In modern large-scale robot control, behavioral cloning (BC)—which mimics expert trajectories via supervised learning—serves as the foundational paradigm. However, when BC is trained on complex real-world data collected by humans, many bizarre, counterintuitive phenomena have been observed. For instance, test success rates often continue to rise even as validation loss worsens and the model overfits; open-loop control (action chunking), which predicts several steps ahead and executes them blindly, performs far better than closed-loop control reacting in real time; and feeding past observation history, which should provide more information, often degrades performance instead.

Attempting to study these phenomena academically and quantitatively on physical robots was hampered by low trial repeatability and the high cost of collecting human demonstrations, preventing controlled experiments that cleanly isolate variables. On the other hand, traditional simulator environments and scripted trajectories failed to reproduce these phenomena. The trajectories generated by conventional scripted policies diverged significantly from the unique structure of human demonstrations.

In this work, the authors developed 'OCBench', a simulator environment that mimics crucial structural characteristics of human demonstration trajectories (such as locally narrow trajectory distributions, highly non-Markovian temporal correlations, and smooth randomness). OCBench runs on GPU-parallel MuJoCo powered by NVIDIA Warp (MJWarp), generating up to 200,000 steps per second on a single H100 GPU. This enables streaming model training with virtually 'infinite data', allowing algorithmic investigations in extreme regimes free from data-scarcity bias.

sections.heading: Where prior BC analyses and benchmarks fell short
sections.summary: While modern robot BC relies heavily on flow matching and action chunking, prior analytical studies depended on small-scale real-world datasets of tens to hundreds of episodes. Synthetic environments existed, but failed to capture the core properties of human demonstrations.
sections.details:
Modern large-scale robot learning is primarily driven by BC using diffusion models or flow matching. Combining large Transformers with flow matching has demonstrated impressive results, and this paper also focuses primarily on flow-based BC.

Prior analytical studies have investigated BC failure modes and behaviors, such as test-time distribution shift (the covariate shift problem tackled by DAgger), action chunking, and incorporating history. However, most prior empirical studies relied on limited human demonstration datasets consisting of only 50 to 300 episodes. As a result, they could not disentangle whether observed phenomena were due to data scarcity or represented fundamental properties of BC itself.

Meanwhile, simulation benchmarks like Robomimic, D4RL, OGBench, and MimicGen exist. However, while MimicGen stitches and amplifies a small set of human trajectories, OCBench generates trajectories with human-like properties entirely from scratch via fully programmatic scripts. Furthermore, conventional scripted datasets mostly added simple Gaussian noise, failing to replicate real-world phenomena. OCBench is the first benchmark to combine structural reproduction of human demonstrations with extreme GPU-parallel generation speeds.

sections.heading: The four mysteries puzzling practitioners
sections.summary: This section outlines four empirical mysteries observed in the field: benefits of overfitting, open-loop superiority, demand for huge models, and sensitivity to feature scaling. It also discusses why conventional synthetic data failed to reproduce them.
sections.details:
This study focuses on four empirical 'mysteries' widely reported in real-world robotics and autonomous driving:

- **Mystery 1: Overfitting is not necessarily bad**: Task success rate continues to increase even while validation loss degrades and overfitting progresses. Furthermore, an inverted phenomenon has been reported where training on a smaller dataset yields a higher success rate than training on a larger one drawn from the same distribution.
- **Mystery 2: Open-loop is often better than closed-loop**: Even in environments with zero inference latency, step-by-step closed-loop control fails almost completely, whereas partial open-loop control using action chunking works remarkably well. Adding observation history does not fix this.
- **Mystery 3: Policies should be very large**: While simple low-dimensional state tasks on conventional synthetic data can be solved with an MLP of a few hundred thousand parameters, cloning human demonstrations requires massive models on the order of 100M parameters.
- **Mystery 4: Features matter even with enough data**: Simply changing the scaling of the state representation (multiplying specific dimensions by a factor) drastically alters performance, despite containing the exact same information.

In conventional synthetic benchmarks (such as OGBench and Robomimic MG), the performance gap between closed-loop and open-loop was small, and performance saturated quickly with small models. The authors identified the root cause: conventional scripted trajectories relied on Gaussian noise with weak temporal correlations, resulting in action statistics dominated by saturated boundary values (-1 or +1). This insight directly guided the design of OCBench.

sections.heading: Inside the architecture of OCBench
sections.summary: OCBench reproduces key properties of human demonstrations—narrow distribution, strong temporal correlation, and semantic diversity—using cubic Hermite spline interpolation. It offers 28 tasks based on a UR5e arm, generating 200,000 steps per second on a GPU.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Scripted Policies and Datasets
The authors defined the core properties of human demonstrations as: (1) locally very narrow trajectory distributions (not dispersing chaotically like Gaussian noise), (2) highly non-Markovian temporal correlations, and (3) rich semantic diversity across different grasp poses and approaches.

To replicate these mathematically, piecewise $C^1$-continuous Hermite splines (Catmull-Rom tangent matching) were adopted as the backbone for trajectory generation. Random control points are sampled across phases such as grasping, lifting, and carrying, and smoothly interpolated. Waypoints, grasp angles and directions, contact points, movement speeds, gripper roll and pitch, trajectory curvature, and even high-level task strategies are extensively randomized. Furthermore, intentional occasional failures and recovery behaviors are incorporated into the robot's motions.

### 4.2 Provided Tasks
OCBench provides 28 tasks across 5 environment suites based on a UR5e manipulator. The simulation runs at 50 Hz, with a 7-dimensional action space of relative joint displacements. To support even faster experimental iterations, lightweight versions (lite tasks) running at 10 Hz with shorter horizons, as well as pixel-based tasks learning from multi-view images, are also provided.

sections.heading: Investigating the four mysteries in OCBench: what holds and what fails
sections.summary: Using OCBench's streaming setup, four mysteries were systematically investigated in controlled experiments. The authors reveal how overfitting may prevent distribution shifts, why temporal correlation makes open-loop control succeed, why massive parameter counts are needed, and how feature scaling affects generalization.
sections.details:
The baseline experimental setup uses flow matching with action chunking (default chunk size of 25), executed open-loop at test time without replanning.

### 5.1 Mystery 1: Why is Overfitting Not Bad?
The test success rate was significantly higher for the final model trained hundreds of thousands of steps past the point of minimum validation loss (flow loss). Furthermore, the 'size inversion' phenomenon was reproduced: training on 10k episodes achieved statistically significantly higher performance than training on 30k or 50k episodes from the same distribution.
- **Hypothesis Testing**: The authors evaluated whether this could be explained by loss metrics (action MSE rather than velocity loss), but MSE still could not explain the inversion. An ultra-large 540M-parameter model also did not eliminate the phenomenon, ruling out insufficient network capacity. The authors propose the 'neural nearest neighbor' hypothesis: overfitting forces the model to strictly trace the nearest dataset segment, protecting it from compounding errors and distribution shifts at test time.

### 5.2 Mystery 2: Why Does Open-Loop Dominate Closed-Loop?
Even with zero inference latency, 1-step closed-loop control failed almost completely (near 0%), whereas open-loop control with chunk size 25 performed overwhelmingly better.
- **Hypothesis Testing**: To test the compounding sampling error hypothesis, they evaluated a delayed closed-loop policy conditioned on past states, $\pi(a_t \mid s_{t-k})$, which achieved high success rates despite sampling at every step. Additionally, when demonstrations were Markovianized (re-planning at each step to destroy temporal correlations), the performance gap between closed-loop and open-loop shrunk substantially. Thus, the inability of closed-loop policies to capture the strong non-Markovian nature (temporal dependencies) of human demonstrations is the primary cause of closed-loop failure.
- **The Trap of Observation History**: Feeding past observation sequences $s_{t-24:t}$ into closed-loop policies lowered training and validation losses, yet drastically worsened test-time performance. This is attributed to vulnerability to distribution shifts from increased input dimensionality and causal confusion from merely copying previous actions.

### 5.3 Mystery 3: Why Do Policies Need to Be Huge?
On conventional synthetic data, performance saturated at 500k parameters ($[512]\times 3$ MLP). In contrast, on OCBench, performance continued to scale with model size up to around 500M parameters ($[8192]\times 8$ ResMLP).
- **Hypothesis Testing**: To test whether this was due to variance in flow matching, actions were discretized into tokens via FSQ (Finite Scalar Quantization) and predicted using an autoregressive Transformer; performance still scaled steadily with model size. This indicates that capturing the complexity and diversity of human-like motions demands hundreds of millions of parameters, even on state-based manipulation tasks.

### 5.4 Mystery 4: Why Does Feature Scaling Matter?
Using infinite streaming data, the authors compared four feature scalings with identical information content (manual tuning, standardization, and xyz coordinates scaled by 0.1x / 10x). Despite identical training loss and validation MSE, task success rates varied dramatically.
- **Mechanism**: Measuring the test-time action difference from the scripted policy (test MSE) revealed completely different behaviors across feature scalings. How the model weights features during representation learning dictates its inductive bias and generalization direction in unvisited states.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook: a virtual sandbox accelerating real-world robotics
sections.summary: OCBench accurately reproduces complex real-world BC phenomena in simulation, enabling rigorous scientific inquiry. With extensions to offline RL envisioned, it serves as an agile testbed for validating hypotheses prior to real-robot experiments.
sections.details:
This study introduced OCBench, a GPU-parallel robotic manipulation benchmark that reproduces the structural properties of human demonstrations, enabling the replication and analysis of real-world BC mysteries.

While this paper focused on BC analysis, OCBench is also well-suited for offline reinforcement learning (RL). Its scripted policies can generate trajectories at varying speeds mimicking operator proficiency (the fastest being roughly 2x faster than the slowest), enabling RL evaluation focused not only on success rate but also on throughput (task completion speed). Ground-truth subtask boundaries are also included, which can aid hierarchical control research.

Of course, no matter how carefully scripted, artificial trajectories cannot perfectly replicate actual humans. Final validation must ultimately be conducted on real robots and real data. Nonetheless, OCBench provides a powerful, accessible sandbox for rapidly testing hypotheses and cleanly isolating variables.

sections.heading: Appendix: Environment details and key differences from prior benchmarks
sections.summary: Detailed specifications of the five environments (block, chamber, switch, hanoi, bowling) and quantitative/qualitative comparisons with OGBench and Robomimic MG. The BC mysteries were also confirmed to replicate in pixel-based tasks.
sections.details:
### Details of Provided Environments
- **block (8 tasks)**: Manipulation tasks involving 1 to 4 blocks. Requires placing at target positions, stacking freely, and arranging in grids.
- **chamber (7 tasks)**: Compound environment featuring a drawer, window, and button lock. Features ultra-long horizons up to 5,500 steps, randomized execution orders, and recovery from accidental slips.
- **switch (6 tasks)**: Button manipulation mimicking the Lights Out puzzle. Demonstrations are intentionally non-optimal with exploratory trials, assessing the ability to learn from suboptimal data.
- **hanoi (6 tasks)**: Transferring disks across pegs following Towers of Hanoi rules. Demands high precision due to narrow tolerances, spanning up to 7,000 steps.
- **bowling (1 task)**: Pushing a ball to knock down bowling pins. Tests modeling of unpredictable multi-body contact dynamics.

### Differences from Existing Benchmarks
Comparisons with OGBench and Robomimic MG revealed that on existing benchmarks, the gap between open-loop and closed-loop control was small, and performance saturated around a 256-width MLP. Scripted policies in existing environments produced extreme action distributions clustered at -1 and +1 or uniform distributions, differing fundamentally from smooth human action profiles.

### Replication in Pixel-Based Tasks
Vision-based (pixel) tasks using ConvNeXt V2-N as an image encoder also replicated these BC phenomena: performance gains from overfitting, overwhelming superiority of open-loop control, and the connection between test-time MSE and generalization.

takeaways: Overfitting in BC is not inherently harmful; strictly tracking nearest-neighbor demonstration trajectories may play a beneficial role in preventing test-time distribution shifts (covariate shift).

Action chunking excels primarily because closed-loop policies fail to capture the strong non-Markovian nature (temporal correlation) of human demonstrations, not simply because of compounding sampling error.
Feeding past observation history can cause test performance to collapse despite lower training loss, due to causal confusion and vulnerability to distribution shifts from higher input dimensionality.
In BC with human-like demonstrations, scaling policies to hundreds of millions of parameters remains beneficial even for low-dimensional state tasks, justifying massive action experts in VLAs.
limitations: While OCBench scripts closely mimic human demonstration properties, they do not perfectly match actual human cognitive and physiological behavior; ultimate verification still requires real hardware data.
Certain mysteries—such as performance improving when reducing dataset size—are successfully reproduced but lack a complete theoretical explanation.
Because the analysis primarily focuses on flow matching and diffusion models, it remains open whether identical trends appear across other generative architectures or different loss formulations.
